newsitem.title: BOSNIA: NATO patrol spots war crimes suspect.
newsitem.headline: NATO patrol spots war crimes suspect.

text.p: NATO peacekeeping soldiers spotted a man who resembled a war crimes suspect during a patrol in central Bosnia but chose not to arrest him, alliance spokesmen said on Thursday.

Two soldiers in the NATO-led Stabilisation Force (SFOR) saw a man on a street in the central town of Vitez who they believed was Pero Skopljak, a Bosnian Croat indicted by the U.N. war crimes tribunal in the Hague, a NATO spokesman said.
"They saw him walking on a bridge in Vitez," said Major Jan Joosten, a spokesman for SFOR.

The two soldiers drove to a NATO base in nearby Novi Travnik and checked a poster with photos of war crimes suspects. They concluded they had properly identified Skopljak but chose not to drive back to Vitez, Joosten said.

Travelling 20 km (12 miles) back to Vitez to look for Skopljak would have amounted to a "manhunt", which runs against NATO policy on war crimes suspects, said another alliance officer stationed in central Bosnia.
"To go back to Vitez would have meant a manhunt and that's not in our mandate," said the officer, who asked not to be named.
The source said the two soldiers involved were part of the Dutch contingent in SFOR.

NATO commanders, anxious to avoid a possible backlash against their troops, say SFOR soldiers will arrest indicted war criminals if they encounter them during the course of their normal duties but have ruled out tracking down suspects.
One of the most prominent war crimes suspects, former Bosnian Serb president Radovan Karadzic, was spotted last month by U.N. police monitors in a motorcade in Pale, outside Sarajevo.
Critics say post-war reconciliation between Bosnia's Moslems, Croats and Serbs will be impossible unless indicted war criminals are extradited to the Hague.
Skopljak is one of several Bosnian Croat militia members accused of orchestrating ethnic expulsions in the central Lasva valley during the Moslem-Croat war in Bosnia.
A Sarajevo newspaper, Dnevni Avaz, reported on Thursday that Skopljak and two other Croat war crimes suspects are believed to be living in Croat-held territory in Bosnia.

The newspaper, citing anonymous sources, said Dario Kordic, also indicted for his role in alleged war crimes in the Lasva valley, had moved back to western Bosnia from the Croatian capital Zagreb because his presence there had proved embarassing for the Croatian government.
